notes:
Basics

  • $I = \dfrac{q}{t} = nAev_d$; drift velocity $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$ (order $10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$ in metals). Mobility $\mu = v_d/E$, unit m$^2$V$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$.
  • Ohm's law $V = IR$; $R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}$; $\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}$; conductivity $\sigma = 1/\rho$ (S m$^{-1}$).
  • Wire stretched to $n$ times its length (volume constant): $R' = n^2 R$.
  • $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$. $\alpha$ is positive for metals, negative for semiconductors and insulators; nearly zero for manganin/constantan.

Combinations

  • Series: $R = R_1 + R_2 + \dots$; Parallel: $\dfrac1R = \dfrac1{R_1} + \dfrac1{R_2} + \dots$. $n$ equal resistors: series/parallel ratio $= n^2$.

Cells

  • $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}$; terminal voltage $V = E - Ir$ (discharging), $V = E + Ir$ (charging).
  • $n$ cells in series: $I = \dfrac{nE}{R + nr}$; $m$ cells in parallel: $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r/m}$. Max power to external $R$ when $R = r$.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • Junction rule (charge conservation): $\sum I = 0$. Loop rule (energy conservation): $\sum IR = \sum E$.

Wheatstone bridge & instruments

  • Balanced: $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$; no current through galvanometer.
  • Metre bridge: $\dfrac{R}{X} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$.
  • Potentiometer: $E \propto l$; $\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}$; internal resistance $r = R\left(\dfrac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right)$. Draws no current at balance, hence better than a voltmeter. Sensitivity ↑ when potential gradient ↓ (longer wire).

Power

  • $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$. Bulb: $R = V_{rated}^2/P_{rated}$. Bulbs in series: lower-wattage bulb glows brighter.
  • Colour code: Black Brown Red Orange Yellow Green Blue Violet Grey White (0–9). Gold ±5%, silver ±10%, none ±20%.

Exam tip

Highest-weightage chapter in 2nd PUC physics (3–4 questions). Practise metre bridge, potentiometer and cell combination numericals till they take under a minute.

questions.q: A wire of resistance $R$ is stretched uniformly so that its length doubles. Its new resistance is
questions.explanation: Volume is constant, so area halves when length doubles. $R' = \rho\dfrac{2l}{A/2} = 4R$.
questions.trick: Stretched $n\times$ in length (volume fixed) → resistance goes up $n^2\times$.

questions.q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 $\Omega$ is connected to an external resistance of 4 $\Omega$. The terminal voltage of the cell is
questions.trick: Terminal V $=IR$, computed from $I=E/(R+r)$ — quicker than $E-Ir$ here.

questions.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, $P = 2\,\Omega$, $Q = 4\,\Omega$ and $R = 3\,\Omega$. The value of $S$ is
questions.explanation: $P/Q = R/S \Rightarrow S = QR/P = 4\times3/2 = 6\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Wheatstone balance: cross-multiply $P/Q=R/S$, solve for the unknown arm.

questions.q: In a metre bridge, a resistance of 4 $\Omega$ in the left gap balances an unknown resistance in the right gap at 40 cm from the left end. The unknown resistance is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{R}{X} = \dfrac{l}{100-l} \Rightarrow X = 4\times\dfrac{60}{40} = 6\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Metre bridge: $R/X=l/(100-l)$ — balance length from LEFT end goes with $R$.

questions.q: A potentiometer is preferred over a voltmeter for measuring emf because
options: it draws no current from the cell at balance
questions.explanation: At the null point no current flows through the cell, so the reading equals the true emf. A voltmeter always draws some current and reads slightly less than emf.
questions.trick: Potentiometer draws zero current at balance — that's the whole reason it beats a voltmeter.

questions.q: A 100 W, 220 V bulb has a resistance of
questions.trick: Bulb resistance: $R=V_{rated}^2/P_{rated}$ — always use rated values, not actual.

questions.q: A carbon resistor has colour bands red, violet, orange, gold. Its resistance is
questions.explanation: Red = 2, violet = 7, orange = $10^3$ → $27\times10^3 = 27$ k$\Omega$; gold = ±5%.
questions.trick: Colour code: 1st-2nd digits, 3rd=multiplier power of 10, 4th=tolerance.

questions.q: Three resistors each of resistance $R$ give equivalent resistance $R_s$ in series and $R_p$ in parallel. $R_s/R_p$ is
questions.explanation: $R_s = 3R$, $R_p = R/3$, ratio $= 9$. In general $n^2$.
questions.trick: Equal resistors: series/parallel ratio is always $n^2$ for $n$ resistors.

questions.q: The drift velocity of free electrons in a conductor is $v$ when a current $I$ flows. If both the radius of the wire and the current are doubled, the drift velocity becomes
questions.explanation: $v_d = I/(nAe)$. Area becomes 4 times, current 2 times → $v_d' = 2v/4 = v/2$.
questions.trick: $v_d\propto I/A$: area scales as $r^2$, so doubling both gives $v_d\to v_d/2$.

questions.q: $n$ identical cells, each of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$, are connected in series across an external resistance $R$. The current is
questions.explanation: Total emf $nE$, total internal resistance $nr$: $I = \dfrac{nE}{R+nr}$.
questions.trick: $n$ cells in series: emf and internal resistance both scale by $n$: $nE/(R+nr)$.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a consequence of conservation of
questions.explanation: Charge cannot accumulate at a junction, so the total current in equals the total current out. The loop rule follows from conservation of energy.
questions.trick: Junction rule = charge conservation; loop rule = energy conservation — don't swap them.

questions.q: The SI unit of mobility of charge carriers is
questions.trick: Mobility unit: $v_d/E$ = (m/s)/(V/m) = m$^2$V$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$, build it from definition.

questions.q: In a potentiometer experiment, the balancing length for a cell is 240 cm on open circuit. When a 2 $\Omega$ resistor is connected across the cell, the balancing length becomes 120 cm. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.explanation: $r = R\left(\dfrac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{240}{120} - 1\right) = 2\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: $r=R(l_1/l_2-1)$ — plug open-circuit and loaded balancing lengths directly.

questions.q: Two bulbs of 60 W and 100 W (both rated 220 V) are connected in series to a 220 V supply. Then
questions.explanation: In series the same current flows; power $= I^2R$. The 60 W bulb has higher resistance ($V^2/P$), so it dissipates more power and glows brighter.
questions.tip: Series → higher resistance (lower wattage) bulb brighter. Parallel → higher wattage brighter.
questions.trick: Series circuit: LOWER wattage bulb has higher R, so it glows brighter.

questions.q: The resistance of a conductor is 5 $\Omega$ at 50°C and 6 $\Omega$ at 100°C. Its resistance at 0°C is
questions.explanation: $R = R_0(1+\alpha t)$: $5 = R_0(1+50\alpha)$, $6 = R_0(1+100\alpha)$. Dividing: $6(1+50\alpha) = 5(1+100\alpha) \Rightarrow 1 = 200\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = 1/200$. Then $R_0 = 5/(1+0.25) = 4\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Two $R$-$t$ equations, $R=R_0(1+\alpha t)$: solve simultaneously for $\alpha$ then $R_0$.

questions.q: Maximum power is delivered by a cell of internal resistance $r$ to an external resistance $R$ when
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{E^2R}{(R+r)^2}$ is maximum when $R = r$ (maximum power transfer theorem); then $P_{max} = E^2/4r$.
questions.trick: Max power transfer: always $R=r$, giving $P_{max}=E^2/4r$.

questions.q: The electrical resistivity $\rho$ of a conductor depends on
options: the material of the conductor and its temperature
area of cross-section of the conductor
questions.explanation: Resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material, depending on its nature and temperature, unlike resistance which also depends on length and area.
questions.trick: Resistivity depends only on material and temperature — never on length or area.

questions.q: Current density $J$ at a point in a conductor is defined as
options: current per unit area of cross-section, in the direction of current flow
questions.explanation: Current density is a vector, $J=I/A$, representing current flowing per unit cross-sectional area in the direction of current flow.
questions.trick: Current density $J=I/A$ is a vector along current flow — not per length or volume.

questions.q: A copper wire of cross-sectional area $1\times10^{-6}$ m$^2$ carries a current of 1.6 A. If the free electron density is $n=8\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$, the drift velocity of the electrons is (take $e=1.6\times10^{-19}$ C)
questions.explanation: $v_d=\dfrac{I}{nAe}=\dfrac{1.6}{8\times10^{28}\times10^{-6}\times1.6\times10^{-19}}=\dfrac{1.6}{1.28\times10^{4}}\approx1.25\times10^{-4}$ m/s.
questions.trick: $v_d=I/(nAe)$ — plug all four given values directly, watch powers of 10.

questions.q: A battery of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is being charged by a current $I$ flowing into it. Its terminal voltage is
questions.explanation: While charging, the terminal voltage exceeds the emf by the drop across internal resistance: $V=E+Ir$ (as opposed to $V=E-Ir$ while discharging).
questions.trick: Charging: terminal voltage is $E+Ir$ (exceeds emf); discharging: $E-Ir$.

questions.q: Two identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 1 $\Omega$, are connected in parallel across an external resistance of 2 $\Omega$. The current through the external resistance is
questions.explanation: For $m$ identical cells in parallel, $I=\dfrac{E}{R+r/m}=\dfrac{1.5}{2+0.5}=0.6$ A.
questions.trick: Identical cells in parallel: use $I=E/(R+r/m)$ with $m$ = number of cells.

questions.q: A 4 $\Omega$ resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of 6 $\Omega$ and 3 $\Omega$ resistors. The total resistance of the combination is
questions.explanation: Parallel: $\dfrac{6\times3}{6+3}=2\,\Omega$; in series with 4 $\Omega$: total $=4+2=6\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Solve the parallel branch first, then simply add the series resistor.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's loop (voltage) rule for any closed loop in a circuit is a consequence of conservation of
questions.explanation: The loop rule ($\sum IR = \sum E$) follows from conservation of energy: the net change in potential around any closed loop is zero.
questions.trick: Loop rule ($\sum IR=\sum E$) comes from energy conservation, not charge.

questions.q: The sensitivity of a potentiometer (its ability to measure small potential differences) can be increased by
options: decreasing the potential gradient along the wire (e.g. using a longer wire)
increasing the potential gradient along the wire
increasing the current through the wire
decreasing the length of the potentiometer wire
questions.explanation: A smaller potential gradient ($E$ per unit length) means a larger balancing length for a given potential difference, allowing finer (more sensitive) measurement; this is achieved with a longer wire.
questions.trick: Lower potential gradient (longer wire) = higher potentiometer sensitivity.

questions.q: An ideal ammeter should have
options: resistance equal to the galvanometer resistance
resistance equal to the circuit resistance
questions.explanation: An ideal ammeter, connected in series, should have zero resistance so that it does not alter the current it is measuring.
questions.trick: Ideal ammeter: zero resistance (in series, shouldn't add resistance).

questions.q: An ideal voltmeter should have
options: resistance equal to that of the component across which it is connected
questions.explanation: An ideal voltmeter, connected in parallel, should have infinite resistance so that it draws no current and does not change the potential difference being measured.
questions.trick: Ideal voltmeter: infinite resistance (in parallel, shouldn't draw current).

questions.q: An electrical appliance rated 2000 W is used for 3 hours daily. The energy consumed in 5 days, in kWh, is
questions.explanation: Energy $= P\times t = 2\,\text{kW}\times3\,\text{h}\times5\,\text{days} = 30$ kWh.
questions.trick: Energy = power(kW) $\times$ hours/day $\times$ days — straight multiplication, keep units in kWh.

questions.q: A current of 2 A flows through a resistor of 50 $\Omega$ for 1 minute. The heat generated is
questions.explanation: $P=I^2R=2^2\times50=200$ W; heat $=P\times t=200\times60=12000$ J.
questions.trick: Heat $=I^2Rt$ — square the current, don't forget minutes to seconds.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT obey Ohm's law (is a non-ohmic device)?
options: a metallic wire at constant temperature
questions.explanation: A semiconductor diode has a non-linear V-I characteristic and does not obey Ohm's law; metallic conductors at constant temperature are ohmic.
questions.trick: Non-ohmic = non-linear V-I graph; diodes, not simple resistors or metal wires.

questions.q: As temperature increases, the resistance of a pure semiconductor
questions.explanation: In semiconductors, increasing temperature releases more charge carriers, increasing conductivity and hence decreasing resistance — opposite to the behaviour of metals.
questions.trick: Semiconductors: resistance DECREASES with rising temperature — opposite trend to metals.

questions.q: A superconductor is a material whose electrical resistance
options: becomes exactly zero below a certain critical temperature
questions.explanation: Below its critical temperature, a superconductor offers zero resistance to the flow of current.
questions.trick: Superconductor = exactly zero resistance below its critical temperature, not just low.

questions.q: The electromotive force (emf) of a cell is defined as the
options: work done per unit charge by the source in driving charge around the complete circuit, including through the cell itself
resistance offered by the cell to current flow
maximum current the cell can supply
potential difference across its terminals when maximum current flows
questions.explanation: EMF is the total work done per unit charge by the source in moving charge around the entire circuit; it equals the terminal voltage only when no current flows (open circuit).
questions.trick: EMF = work per unit charge round the WHOLE circuit, including inside the cell.

questions.q: A cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is short-circuited (external resistance = 0). The current drawn from the cell is
questions.explanation: With $R=0$, $I=E/(R+r)=E/r$, the maximum current the cell can deliver.
questions.trick: Short circuit ($R=0$): current is simply $E/r$, the cell's maximum output.

questions.q: Two resistors of 2 $\Omega$ and 3 $\Omega$ are connected in series across a 10 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The voltage across the 3 $\Omega$ resistor is
questions.explanation: $I=10/(2+3)=2$ A; voltage across 3 $\Omega$ $=IR=2\times3=6$ V (voltage divider).
questions.trick: Voltage divider in series: $V_i=I\times R_i$, using the same series current throughout.

questions.q: Two resistors of 2 $\Omega$ and 3 $\Omega$ are connected in parallel, and the combination carries a total current of 5 A. The current through the 2 $\Omega$ resistor is
questions.explanation: By the current divider rule, the current through one branch is inversely proportional to its resistance: $I_2 = I_{total}\times\dfrac{R_3}{R_2+R_3}=5\times\dfrac{3}{5}=3$ A.
questions.trick: Current divider: current splits in INVERSE proportion to resistance in that branch.

questions.q: The SI unit of electrical conductivity is
questions.explanation: Conductivity $\sigma=1/\rho$ has SI unit siemens per metre (S/m), the reciprocal of resistivity's unit ($\Omega$ m).
questions.trick: Conductivity unit is S/m — reciprocal of resistivity's $\Omega\cdot$m, invert to recall.

questions.q: A copper wire is drawn thinner (its cross-sectional area is reduced) while its length is kept fixed. The resistivity of the copper
options: remains unchanged, since it depends only on the material and temperature
questions.explanation: Resistivity is a material property (depending only on the material and temperature), unaffected by changes in the conductor's dimensions; only the resistance $R=\rho l/A$ changes.
questions.trick: Resistivity is material-only — changing wire dimensions changes $R$, never $\rho$.

questions.q: In a circuit, a 2 $\Omega$ resistor is in series with a parallel combination of 3 $\Omega$ and 6 $\Omega$ resistors, connected to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The current through the 6 $\Omega$ resistor is
questions.explanation: Parallel part: $\dfrac{3\times6}{3+6}=2\,\Omega$; total resistance $=2+2=4\,\Omega$; total current $=12/4=3$ A; voltage across parallel part $=3\times2=6$ V; current through 6 $\Omega$ $=6/6=1$ A.
questions.trick: Reduce parallel branch, find total current, then back-calculate voltage across it for branch currents.

questions.q: In an electrolyte, electric current is carried by
options: both positive and negative ions moving in opposite directions
questions.explanation: In an electrolyte, current is due to the drift of both positive ions (towards the cathode) and negative ions (towards the anode) in opposite directions.
questions.trick: Electrolyte current: BOTH +ve and −ve ions move, in opposite directions — not electrons alone.

questions.q: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the graph of potential difference $V$ versus current $I$ is
options: a curve bending towards the V-axis
a straight line with a positive intercept
a straight line passing through the origin
questions.explanation: Ohm's law, $V=IR$ with constant $R$, gives a straight line through the origin with slope $R$.
questions.trick: Ohmic conductor: $V$-$I$ graph is a straight line through the origin, slope = $R$.
